title: QPILOTS:Efficient Test-Time Q-Steering for Flow Policies

paper.title: QPILOTS : Efficient Test-Time Q-Steering for Flow Policies
paper.abstract:
Abstract Flow-matching and diffusion policies are expressive action generators, but optimizing them with temporal-difference reinforcement learning (RL) remains difficult. Effective policy extraction requires exploiting the critic’s action gradient, yet directly backpropagating this signal through a multi-step denoising process can be numerically unstable.
Existing methods work around this either by discarding gradient information, distilling the policy into a simpler one-step actor, or repeatedly fine-tuning the denoising policy as the critic improves.
We propose QPILOTS , a method that leaves the original policy unmodified and steers the denoising process at inference time. At each denoising step, instead of evaluating the critic on the noisy intermediate action where critic predictions are unreliable, we first project that intermediate state to an estimate of the final clean action and compute the critic gradient there. We introduce two variants: QPILOTS-U uses a fast single-point approximation, while QPILOTS-M draws differentiable posterior samples via a learned auxiliary network. On a standard offline-to-online RL benchmark, QPILOTS achieves the best aggregate performance, reaching an average success rate of 90 % 90\% across 50 tasks. We also apply QPILOTS to steer a large, frozen, pretrained Vision-Language Action (VLA) foundation model, outperforming or matching prior inference-time approaches across six manipulation tasks in simulation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow-matching and diffusion policies have become the de facto standard way to represent complex, multi-modal action distributions in continuous control and vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 32 , 8 , 10 ] and there is sustained interest in improving these policies with downstream rewards [ 43 , 54 , 13 , 30 ] . Formally, this can be framed as behavior-constrained policy learning, where the agent is equipped with a base flow policy π β ​ ( a | s ) \pi_{\beta}(a|s) trained on an offline dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and improves it online with a learned critic, Q Q , without straying too far from the base policy. Recently, Park et al. [42] has shown that the main challenge is to extract this optimal policy from ( π β , Q ) (\pi_{\beta},Q) rather than learning Q Q itself. We refer to this mapping from a base policy and critic to an improved action distribution as policy extraction . An extractor may either modify the policy during training or steer its samples at inference time. For simple reparameterized policies, the critic’s action gradient ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) \nabla_{a}Q(s,a) can guide policy updates. For flow policies, this same signal must pass through a multi-step generation, and backpropagation through the denoising process is often unstable or expensive [ 56 , 48 , 37 ] . To circumvent this instability, prior work distills the original flow policy into a one-step approximation [ 43 , 30 ] or uses finetuning to target the optimal policy [ 47 , 16 , 30 ] . In practice, the former sacrifices expressivity, and the latter requires tuning policy parameters, hindering its scalability to large-capacity models due to the prohibitive computational overhead. This motivates another class of methods to apply guidance during inference , forgoing the need for finetuning. However, in offline-online Reinforcement Learning (RL) benchmarks, they have thus far been outperformed by methods that use finetuning [ 30 ] , and often have limited expressivity [ 13 ] , high cost [ 20 ] , or apply guidance at noisy actions where the critic is not calibrated [ 54 , 30 ] . Addressing these limitations, we introduce QPILOTS (Q-guided Posterior Inference for Learning Off-policy and Test-time Steering). Our main method, QPILOTS-M , builds on Meta Flow Maps (MFM) [ 46 ] to construct an asymptotically unbiased estimator of clean-action Q-value gradients during flow sampling. This allows a standard off-policy critic to steer the base policy without evaluating the critic on noisy intermediate latents. In turn, QPILOTS-M recovers much of the useful gradient information available to training-time extractors without the instability of backpropagating through the full denoising chain or the expressivity loss of one-step distillation. Empirically, we find that QPILOTS achieves the best aggregate score among competitive training-time [ 56 , 43 , 30 ] and inference-time baselines [ 20 , 54 , 13 ] on the OGBench [ 41 ] offline/offline-to-online RL benchmark, establishing it as a powerful solution to policy extraction. We further apply QPILOTS to steer a state-of-the-art pretrained generalist π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 7 ] without modifying the base flow, demonstrating that QPILOTS successfully learns from online interactions even with a behavior Q-value, surpassing or matching other inference-time approaches on 6 6 tasks from the LIBERO-90 suite [ 33 ] . Taken together, our contribution is an efficient inference-time steering recipe that applies RL to flow policies by leveraging clean-space Q-values to guide the intermediate generation process.

sections.heading: Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning.
sections.text: Offline-to-online RL methods leverage offline datasets to pre-train policies and value functions, then fine-tune them through online interaction to improve sample efficiency [ 58 , 28 , 52 , 40 , 53 , 62 , 29 ] . A common recipe uses the same offline RL objective during both phases, with the offline dataset loaded into a replay buffer alongside newly collected transitions [ 5 ] . While purely online methods can treat the offline data as additional off-policy experience, offline pre-training tends to produce stronger results on challenging sparse-reward tasks [ 31 , 30 ] . We adopt this training setup for the critic and focus on the complementary challenge of policy extraction , that is selecting high-value actions with the policy while remaining close to the behavior support [ 18 , 27 , 40 ] . This emphasis follows the observation that policy extraction and test-time generalization can be the limiting factors in offline RL, even when the value function is well-trained [ 42 ] . It also affords our approach inherent deployment flexibility, allowing the same inference-time extractor to be used offline, online, or during fine-tuning.

sections.heading: RL with Diffusion and Flow Policies.
sections.text: Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a dominant policy class in both imitation learning and RL due to their ability to represent complex, multi-modal action distributions [ 24 , 2 , 26 , 21 , 35 , 20 , 12 , 9 , 48 , 10 ] . A central challenge is optimizing these policies against a critic Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) when the generation process involves a multi-step denoising chain. Unlike prior work that categorizes approaches by how the value function is used [ 30 ] , we classify them according to how the base policy is treated during training and inference. Under this lens, existing approaches can be categorized into three strategies. 1. Back-Propagating Through Time (BPTT) offers a straightforward way to use value signals by differentiating the critic through the full denoising chain to maximize Q [ 56 , 21 , 60 ] . Related policy-gradient formulations instead make likelihoods or advantage ratios tractable for flow policies and updating the policy itself [ 37 , 61 ] . While conceptually simple, computing gradients through the long unrolled chain of many-step flows is highly prone to numerical instability [ 43 ] . 2. Policy Fine-Tuning without BPTT avoids full-chain gradients by changing the policy objective. Some methods distill the multi-step flow into a simplified one-step policy, improving stability but giving up part of the original model’s iterative expressivity [ 12 , 43 , 15 , 55 ] . Other methods construct a step-wise training objective that uses critic information at intermediate denoising states. Methods like QAM [ 30 ] , alongside other gradient-approximated or value-weighted variants [ 47 , 16 , 17 ] , construct specialized losses where the critic gradient only passes through the base policy at isolated denoising steps. While these avoid the instability of backprop, they couple the base flow and the critic through a specialized loss and require re-training the policy whenever the critic changes. 3. Inference-time steering modifies the action-generation process at test time without impacting training. DSRL [ 49 , 54 ] trains a noise-space RL policy that perturbs the input latents of a frozen flow. Residual and edit policies [ 25 , 3 , 13 , 59 ] train a separate corrector that acts on completed actions. Best-of- N N [ 20 , 39 , 36 , 4 ] samples N N candidates from the base policy and picks the highest-Q one, scaling poorly with action dimension. All of these consult the critic either after a full action has been produced or via a separately trained auxiliary policy. Our method instead injects a noiseless-action Q-gradient into the Euler integrator at every denoising step, guiding the trajectory mid-integration without training an edit policy or modifying the base flow weights.

sections.heading: 4 QPILOTS : Q-Guided Posterior Inference for Learning Off-Policy and Test-Time Steering
sections.text: We now present our approach for steering a base flow policy with a learned critic. Rather than coupling policy and critic through specialized training-time losses, QPILOTS treats the base flow π β \pi_{\beta} and critic as independent components, each obtained via their own standard objectives, and combines them only at action-generation time. The base flow can be trained from scratch alongside the critic or taken off-the-shelf as a frozen pretrained policy; either way, we add a Q-gradient steering term to the flow’s Euler integrator at inference. Because the base policy is never modified by the critic, any flow-matching policy can be plugged in unchanged, including pretrained policies learned on different data or tasks. We present two instantiations of QPILOTS that trade off bias and computational cost. QPILOTS-U is a Universal-Guidance variant that uses a Tweedie-denoised point estimate, while QPILOTS-M uses Meta Flow Maps to estimate the posterior-tilt gradient from differentiable posterior samples. Algorithm 1 summarizes the shared inference-time procedure underlying both variants.

QPILOTS-U queries v θ v_{\theta} directly from the frozen base flow. QPILOTS-M additionally trains an MFM on LIBERO-90 demonstration data via the GLASS reparameterization of Potaptchik et al. [46] , with the frozen base flow as the conditional teacher. Unlike the original MFM setting, where the auxiliary network is trained on the same dataset that produced the base flow, we have access only to LIBERO-90 (a small subset of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s pretraining mixture, which is not public); the consequences of this mismatch are discussed in Section 5.2 . Full procedures are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Theoretical Guarantees.
sections.text: QPILOTS-M inherits the convergence guarantees of Potaptchik et al. [46] in the RL setting for the idealized sampler that uses exact posterior samples and the unrescaled σ t 2 / 2 \sigma_{t}^{2}/2 drift. Under standard regularity on v θ v_{\theta} , Q ¯ \bar{Q} , the exact posterior sampler, and σ t \sigma_{t} (full assumptions and proof in Appendix B ), the distribution p ^ 1 s \hat{p}_{1}^{s} produced by the the idealized version of Algorithm 1 with K K Euler steps and N N MFM posterior samples per step satisfies W 2 ( p ^ 1 s , π ⋆ ( ⋅ | s ) ) ≤ C ( 1 K + 1 N ) , KL ( p ^ 1 s ∥ π ⋆ ( ⋅ | s ) ) ≤ C ( 1 K + 1 N ) , W_{2}\!\left(\hat{p}_{1}^{s},\,\pi^{\star}(\cdot|s)\right)\leq C\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right),\qquad\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\hat{p}_{1}^{s}\,\|\,\pi^{\star}(\cdot|s)\right)\leq C\!\left(\frac{1}{K}+\frac{1}{N}\right), for some C > 0 C>0 independent of K K and N N . The two error sources, Euler-Maruyama time discretization and Monte Carlo gradient estimation, are controlled independently. QPILOTS-U , which replaces the log-expectation in V t V_{t} with the Tweedie posterior-mean estimate, is Bayes-optimal only when π β \pi_{\beta} is Gaussian; we do not claim a formal guarantee for it.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We evaluate on the OGBench [ 41 ] single-task benchmark, which spans 10 continuous-control domains (5 navigation, 5 manipulation) with 5 tasks per domain, for a total of 50 tasks. Each method first trains for 10 6 10^{6} offline gradient steps on the OGBench dataset, then performs 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} online steps that interleave environment interaction (one gradient update per one environment interaction) with gradient updates over the offline data and an online replay buffer. Manipulation domains use action chunking, navigation domains use single-step actions, per-domain ( H , γ , ρ ) (H,\gamma,\rho) follow Li and Levine [30] (Appendix C.4 ). Critic pessimism is set to ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 throughout, except on the humanoid-maze domains, where we follow Li and Levine [30] and use ρ = 0 \rho=0 . We report mean evaluation success rate at the end of training over 8 8 seeds and 50 50 evaluation episodes per seed, with 95 % 95\% bootstrap CIs across seeds shown in brackets.

sections.heading: Baseline.
sections.text: We group baselines by how they extract a policy from ( π β , Q ) (\pi_{\beta},Q) : (i) Gaussian-policy baseline ReBRAC [ 53 ] (ii) the backprop-based flow extractor FBRAC [ 56 ] , which differentiates through the denoising chain (iii) fine-tuning extractors that update the base flow with a critic-aware objective, including the one-step distillation FQL [ 43 ] , and the adjoint-matching methods QAM and QAM-EDIT (QAM-E) of Li and Levine [30] (iv) inference-time steering methods that wrap a frozen flow, including DSRL [ 54 ] for latent-space policy steering, IFQL [ 20 ] for implicit Q-learning policy extraction with Best-of- N N ( N = 32 N=32 , following Li and Levine [30] ), FEdit [ 13 , 59 ] for post-hoc action refinement via learned Gaussian edit policies, CGQL [ 11 ] for conditional generation via classifier guidance, and the CGQL-MSE/Linex (CGQL-M / CGQL-L) reward-shaping variants of CGQL following Li and Levine [30] . Per-domain hyperparameters for all baselines follow Li and Levine [30] . For our method, we evaluate both QPILOTS-U (Tweedie denoised estimate) and QPILOTS-M (MFM posterior). Both share the base flow, critic ensemble, and Adam optimizer of Li and Levine [30] . QPILOTS-M additionally trains the auxiliary meta flow map. The steering coefficient α \alpha is tuned per domain following Li and Levine [30] ’s protocol, using two tuning tasks per domain (tasks 1 and 4 for navigation, tasks 2 and 4 for manipulation), 4 seeds per configuration. The selected value is reused across all five tasks of that domain and evaluated on 8 fresh seeds. The sweep grid and selected values are in Appendix C.4 .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Both variants lead in aggregate online score ( QPILOTS-M at 90%, QPILOTS-U at 89%), and are especially performant on the humanoid tasks, improving by 25 absolute percentage points over the closest baseline on humanoid-large . QPILOTS-U is surprisingly effective online given its simplicity, beating much more elaborate methods such as QAM-E, though it slightly underperforms on certain tasks offline. QPILOTS-M closes this offline performance gap by replacing the point estimate with the MFM posterior ( Eq. 16 ). We hypothesize that accurate posterior estimates may matter more offline where the replay buffer’s action coverage is limited. QPILOTS significantly outperforms CGQL-Linex and DSRL, likely owing at least partially to our method’s ability to use a critic directly rather than distilling it into an auxiliary critic that operates over noised actions. Per-task learning curves across all 50 tasks are reported in Appendix C.4 .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We test whether both QPILOTS variants can steer a large frozen pretrained base policy, a regime where full fine-tuning is impractical because the base flow has billions of parameters. We use the official π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO checkpoint of Black et al. [7] , pretrained on a large closed-source robotics mixture and then finetuned on LIBERO-40, as the frozen base flow. We evaluate on six tasks from the larger LIBERO-90 suite [ 33 ] on which π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s zero-shot success rate is between 5 and 50 percent. Per-task descriptions are in Appendix C.4 . For QPILOTS-M , we distill the auxiliary meta flow map on the public LIBERO-90 demonstrations ( Section 4 ), keeping the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO weights frozen. Each method runs 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} online environment steps with action chunking matching the base policy. We report results over 5 5 seeds with 95 % 95\% seed-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We follow DSRL’s [ 54 ] simulation setup, but switch to SARSA targets in place of Bellman targets. Constructing a ′ ∼ π ⋆ ( ⋅ | s ′ ) a^{\prime}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot|s^{\prime}) for the off-policy target would require sampling from π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} inside every critic update, which is prohibitive at 3 3 B parameters. SARSA reuses the buffer’s stored a ′ a^{\prime} and avoids this cost. We also conduct a value learning ablation study (Appendix D.2 ) to show that SARSA outperforms other feasible approaches (e.g., IQL, Monte-Carlo, one-step distillation) in LIBERO.

sections.heading: Baselines and Hyperparameters.
sections.text: We compare both QPILOTS variants against DSRL [ 54 ] , Best-of- N N (BoN, N = 5 N=5 ) action selection under the learned critic, EXPO [ 13 ] , and CGQL-LinEx [ 43 ] . All baselines other than DSRL share the same SARSA critic for fairness. We tune one knob per method per task. For DSRL we sweep the action magnitude b W b_{W} over { 1 , 2 , 3 } \{1,2,3\} , matching Wagenmaker et al. [54] . For QPILOTS and CGQL-LinEx we tune the steering coefficient α \alpha over { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } \{0.1,0.2,0.3\} . Selected per-task values are listed in Table 4 . We also include SAC [ 19 ] as a from-scratch baseline; it achieves negligible performance within the 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} -step online budget.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 2 shows per-task online learning curves at 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} steps. Per-task end-of-training detailed success rates are tabulated in Appendix C.4 . QPILOTS-U improves over the frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} base on all six tasks and is the best method on five of six (tasks 26, 31, 38, 60, 64), with the gap over the strongest baseline DSRL ranging from 4 % 4\% on task 60 (within the seed-level bootstrap CIs) to 55 % 55\% on task 64. BoN, EXPO, and CGQL-LinEx, which either lack a directional gradient signal or steer in noise space, plateau well below the steering methods. QPILOTS-M tracks QPILOTS-U on most tasks and beats it on task 59, but does not improve over QPILOTS-U in aggregate on this benchmark. One likely reason is that MFM theory assumes the auxiliary network is distilled on the same data mixture that produced the base flow [ 46 ] . π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s pretraining mixture is closed-source and the public LIBERO-90 demonstrations only partially overlaps with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s training data. The resulting distillation gap might explain why the simpler Tweedie estimate of QPILOTS-U is more performant here. Figure 2: LIBERO Online RL. Per-task success rate over training for the LIBERO benchmark. Curves are time-weighted EMA-smoothed means over 5 5 seeds; shaded bands show seed-level 95 % 95\% bootstrap CIs. Per-task descriptions, hyperparameters, and end-of-training numbers are in Section C.4 .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: We present QPILOTS , an inference-time recipe for applying RL to flow policies that injects a clean-action Q-gradient into the Euler integrator at every denoising step, leaving the base flow and the critic to be trained with off-the-shelf objectives. Our main variant, QPILOTS-M , uses a Meta Flow Map to draw differentiable posterior samples, yielding a posterior-gradient estimator that inherits the asymptotic convergence guarantees of Potaptchik et al. [46] under the true-posterior idealization. QPILOTS-U provides a lightweight alternative by replacing posterior sampling with a Tweedie point estimate. On OGBench offline-to-online, both variants outperform training-time extractors and prior inference-time steering methods, reaching 90 % 90\% aggregate success across 50 50 tasks; on LIBERO with the frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} generalist, QPILOTS improves over the zero-shot base on every evaluated task and surpasses DSRL on average.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work.
sections.text: Similar to previous work, the steering coefficient α \alpha requires manual tuning per domain (or per task on LIBERO). The gradient rescaling in Eq. 17 avoids the singular σ t 2 / 2 \sigma_{t}^{2}/2 schedule but does not eliminate the need to pick a magnitude, and an adaptive choice tied to local critic curvature is a natural next step. We also see two promising extensions. One is to train a residual edit-flow analogue of QPILOTS-M in the spirit of QAM-E to further push performance. The second is to bring offline-trained value functions to large VLAs, where an offline-pretrained Q Q would take advantage of our method’s critic-agnostic nature, which extends the online setting in this work.

We satisfy the assumption operationally by batch-normalizing Q ¯ \bar{Q} across the minibatch before exponentiating and clipping τ ⋅ Q ¯ norm \tau\cdot\bar{Q}_{\mathrm{norm}} to a fixed interval (Section 4 ), which keeps the tilt scalar bounded with constants independent of the absolute Q-scale. Strictly speaking, batch normalization makes the tilt scalar depend on the empirical batch distribution and therefore non-stationary across training, which is outside the iid setting analyzed in Proposition C.4; we treat the resulting bound as a per-batch guarantee rather than a uniform one. Assumption 3 requires a bounded diffusion schedule; the theoretical schedule σ t 2 = 2 ​ ( 1 − t ) / t \sigma_{t}^{2}=2(1-t)/t violates the upper bound as t → 0 t\to 0 (where σ t → ∞ \sigma_{t}\to\infty ) and the lower bound as t → 1 t\to 1 (where σ t → 0 \sigma_{t}\to 0 ). We skip steering at t = 0 t=0 (Section 4 ) to control the upper end, and–following standard practice [ Potaptchik et al., 2026 ] –the formal result applies to the process stopped at t = 1 − ε t=1-\varepsilon to control the lower end. We note that the constant C C depends on the Lipschitz constants of the critic and MFM and may scale exponentially with the action dimension [ Potaptchik et al., 2026 ] . The gradient rescaling used in our practical algorithm ( Eq. 17 ) replaces the σ t 2 / 2 \sigma_{t}^{2}/2 factor with a drift-magnitude-matching heuristic, which targets the same tilted distribution but falls outside the formal SDE analysis; we find it to be more stable empirically.

sections.text: The per-step computational overhead of inference-time steering (Algorithm 1 ) is a single forward-backward through v θ v_{\theta} and the critic for QPILOTS-U , and K K forward passes through the MFM and critic plus one backward pass for QPILOTS-M –all single-step evaluations with no inner rollouts.

sections.heading: C.1 Architecture
sections.text: In OGBench experiments, all networks are MLPs with hidden dimensions ( 512,512,512,512 ) (512,512,512,512) and SiLU activations. The base velocity field v θ ​ ( x t , t , s ) v_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s) is an ActorVectorField that concatenates [ s , x t , FF ⁡ ( t ) ] [s,x_{t},\mathrm{FF}(t)] and outputs a velocity in ℝ H ⋅ A \mathbb{R}^{H\cdot A} , where FF ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{FF}(\cdot) is a 64-dim Fourier-feature embedding and H H is the action-chunking horizon. The critic is a J = 10 J{=}10 -ensemble of Value networks (LayerNorm enabled) with pessimism weight ρ \rho (Section 4 ). The Meta Flow Map v ^ u , w ​ ( x ¯ , t , x t , s ) \hat{v}_{u,w}(\bar{x};\,t,x_{t},s) is an MFMFlowMap : it concatenates [ s , x ¯ , x t , FF ⁡ ( t ) , FF ⁡ ( u ) , FF ⁡ ( w ) ] [s,\bar{x},x_{t},\mathrm{FF}(t),\mathrm{FF}(u),\mathrm{FF}(w)] , with three independent Fourier embeddings for the outer time t t and the auxiliary times ( u , w ) (u,w) . LayerNorm is disabled inside the MFM and base velocity field; its conditioning-action input is passed through unchanged (no t t -gating). We instantiate Polyak-averaged target networks for the critic, the base flow, and the MFM. In LIBERO experiments, the critic Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) uses double-view ( 64 , 64 ) (64,64) images from the global camera and the wrist camera as the pixel inputs. Its network consists of a 4-layer CNN encoder and MLPs with hidden dimensions ( 128,128,128 ) (128,128,128) . We use the same 10-network Q-value ensemble as the critic in OGBench experiments. For baselines like DSRL or EXPO that require an additional Gaussian policy, we use the same structure as the critic and follow the hyperparameters used in OGBench.

sections.text: OGBench experiments use TPU v4-8 hosts. cube-quadruple-play and puzzle-4x4-play-sparse additionally use the OGBench 100M datasets. A full 1.5 × 10 6 1.5\times 10^{6} -step run (offline + online) for one task and four seeds in parallel takes approximately 8 hours for QPILOTS-U and 12 hours for QPILOTS-M , depending on the task (different domains differ widely in evaluation time requirements). sections.heading: D.2 Value Learning Ablation
sections.text: VLA’s slow inference makes standard Bellman target-based TD-learning almost infeasible, as each update requires querying the policy "batch_size" times. To find an alternative, we compare 4 value-learning objectives for the critic on LIBERO-90 task 64: SARSA (we choose for QPILOTS ), Monte Carlo (MC) returns, Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) [ Kostrikov et al., 2022 ] , and Flow Q-Learning (FQL) [ Park et al., 2025b ] . Note that FQL is not used for policy learning. Instead, we still use the steered π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} for inference, but distill the steered π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy into a one-step policy for Q-learning next action query. As shown in Fig. 3 , SARSA reaches a success rate of 90 % 90\% at 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} training steps, outperforming the other 3 approaches. Despite being unbiased, the MC estimator regresses directly against discounted episode returns, which are dominated by large negative rewards in early training, leading to slower initial learning across seeds. IQL and FQL are originally designed for offline RL. However, under the non-stationary replay buffer of our online setting, both methods exhibit instability (high variance), suggesting that current offline value learning approaches still struggle with the continually shifting action distribution. In contrast, SARSA is shown as a pragmatic and effective choice for online critic training under a generalist policy.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2606.14801v1 [cs.LG] 11 Jun 2026 QPILOTS : Efficient Test-Time Q-Steering for Flow Policies Yifan Ruan † † thanks: Corresponding author: yifan@cs.toronto.edu . Chenyang Cao Andreas Burger Ali Pesaranghader Affiliation: University of Toronto Vector Institute LG Electronics Kaveh Kamali Affiliation: University of Toronto Vector Institute LG Electronics Jaehong Kim Affiliation: University of Toronto Vector Institute LG Electronics Nandita Vijaykumar Alan Aspuru-Guzik Igor Gilitschenski Nicholas Rhinehart Abstract Flow-matching and diffusion policies are expressive action generators, but optimizing them with temporal-difference reinforcement learning (RL) remains difficult. Effective policy extraction requires exploiting the critic’s action gradient, yet directly backpropagating this signal through a multi-step denoising process can be numerically unstable. Existing methods work around this either by discarding gradient information, distilling the policy into a simpler one-step actor, or repeatedly fine-tuning the denoising policy as the critic improves. We propose QPILOTS , a method that leaves the original policy unmodified and steers the denoising process at inference time. At each denoising step, instead of evaluating the critic on the noisy intermediate action where critic predictions are unreliable, we first project that intermediate state to an estimate of the final clean action and compute the critic gradient there. We introduce two variants: QPILOTS-U uses a fast single-point approximation, while QPILOTS-M draws differentiable posterior samples via a learned auxiliary network. On a standard offline-to-online RL benchmark, QPILOTS achieves the best aggregate performance, reaching an average success rate of 90 % 90\% across 50 tasks. We also apply QPILOTS to steer a large, frozen, pretrained Vision-Language Action (VLA) foundation model, outperforming or matching prior inference-time approaches across six manipulation tasks in simulation. Right: Aggregated offline-to-online success rates on 50 OGBench tasks [ 41 ] . 1 Introduction Flow-matching and diffusion policies have become the de facto standard way to represent complex, multi-modal action distributions in continuous control and vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 32 , 8 , 10 ] and there is sustained interest in improving these policies with downstream rewards [ 43 , 54 , 13 , 30 ] . Formally, this can be framed as behavior-constrained policy learning, where the agent is equipped with a base flow policy π β ​ ( a | s ) \pi_{ eta}(a|s) trained on an offline dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and improves it online with a learned critic, Q Q , without straying too far from the base policy. Recently, Park et al. [42] has shown that the main challenge is to extract this optimal policy from ( π β , Q ) (\pi_{ eta},Q) rather than learning Q Q itself. We refer to this mapping from a base policy and critic to an improved action distribution as policy extraction . An extractor may either modify the policy during training or steer its samples at inference time. For simple reparameterized policies, the critic’s action gradient ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a )

For flow policies, this same signal must pass through a multi-step generation, and backpropagation through the denoising process is often unstable or expensive [ 56 , 48 , 37 ] . To circumvent this instability, prior work distills the original flow policy into a one-step approximation [ 43 , 30 ] or uses finetuning to target the optimal policy [ 47 , 16 , 30 ] . In practice, the former sacrifices expressivity, and the latter requires tuning policy parameters, hindering its scalability to large-capacity models due to the prohibitive computational overhead. This motivates another class of methods to apply guidance during inference , forgoing the need for finetuning. However, in offline-online Reinforcement Learning (RL) benchmarks, they have thus far been outperformed by methods that use finetuning [ 30 ] , and often have limited expressivity [ 13 ] , high cost [ 20 ] , or apply guidance at noisy actions where the critic is not calibrated [ 54 , 30 ] . Addressing these limitations, we introduce QPILOTS (Q-guided Posterior Inference for Learning Off-policy and Test-time Steering). Our main method, QPILOTS-M , builds on Meta Flow Maps (MFM) [ 46 ] to construct an asymptotically unbiased estimator of clean-action Q-value gradients during flow sampling. This allows a standard off-policy critic to steer the base policy without evaluating the critic on noisy intermediate latents. In turn, QPILOTS-M recovers much of the useful gradient information available to training-time extractors without the instability of backpropagating through the full denoising chain or the expressivity loss of one-step distillation. Empirically, we find that QPILOTS achieves the best aggregate score among competitive training-time [ 56 , 43 , 30 ] and inference-time baselines [ 20 , 54 , 13 ] on the OGBench [ 41 ] offline/offline-to-online RL benchmark, establishing it as a powerful solution to policy extraction. We further apply QPILOTS to steer a state-of-the-art pretrained generalist π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 7 ] without modifying the base flow, demonstrating that QPILOTS successfully learns from online interactions even with a behavior Q-value, surpassing or matching other inference-time approaches on 6 6 tasks from the LIBERO-90 suite [ 33 ] . Taken together, our contribution is an efficient inference-time steering recipe that applies RL to flow policies by leveraging clean-space Q-values to guide the intermediate generation process. 2 Related Work Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning. Offline-to-online RL methods leverage offline datasets to pre-train policies and value functions, then fine-tune them through online interaction to improve sample efficiency [ 58 , 28 , 52 , 40 , 53 , 62 , 29 ] . A common recipe uses the same offline RL objective during both phases, with the offline dataset loaded into a replay buffer alongside newly collected transitions [ 5 ] . While purely online methods can treat the offline data as additional off-policy experience, offline pre-training tends to produce stronger results on challenging sparse-reward tasks [ 31 , 30 ] . We adopt this training setup for the critic and focus on the complementary challenge of policy extraction , that is selecting high-value actions with the policy while remaining close to the behavior support [ 18 , 27 , 40 ] . This emphasis follows the observation that policy extraction and test-time generalization can be the limiting factors in offline RL, even when the value function is well-trained [ 42 ] . It also affords our approach inherent deployment flexibility, allowing the same inference-time extractor to be used offline, online, or during fine-tuning. RL with Diffusion and Flow Policies. Diffusion and flow-matching policies have become a dominant policy class in both imitation learning and RL due to their ability to represent complex, multi-modal action distributions [ 24 , 2 , 26 , 21 , 35 , 20 , 12 , 9 , 48 , 10 ] . A central challenge is optimizing these policies against a critic Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) when the generation process involves a multi-step denoising chain. Unlike prior work that categorizes approaches by how the value function is used [ 30 ] , we classify them according to how the base policy is treated during training and inference. Under this lens, existing approaches can be categorized into three strategies. 1. Back-Propagating Through Time (BPTT) offers a straightforward way to use value signals by differentiating the critic through the full denoising chain to maximize Q [ 56 , 21 , 60 ] . Related policy-gradient formulations instead make likelihoods or advantage ratios tractable for flow policies and updating the policy itself [ 37 , 61 ] . While conceptually simple, computing gradients through the long unrolled chain of many-step flows is highly prone to numerical instability [ 43 ] . 2. Policy Fine-Tuning without BPTT avoids full-chain gradients by changing the policy objective. Some methods distill the multi-step flow into a simplified one-step policy, improving stability but giving up part of the original model’s iterative expressivity [ 12 , 43 , 15 , 55 ] . Other methods construct a step-wise training objective that uses critic information at intermediate denoising states. Methods like QAM [ 30 ] , alongside other gradient-approximated or value-weighted variants [ 47 , 16 , 17 ] , construct specialized losses where the critic gradient only passes through the base policy at isolated denoising steps. While these avoid the instability of backprop, they couple the base flow and the critic through a specialized loss and require re-training the policy whenever the critic changes. 3. Inference-time steering modifies the action-generation process at test time without impacting training. DSRL [ 49 , 54 ] trains a noise-space RL policy that perturbs the input latents of a frozen flow. Residual and edit policies [ 25 , 3 , 13 , 59 ] train a separate corrector that acts on completed actions. Best-of- N N [ 20 , 39 , 36 , 4 ] samples N N candidates from the base policy and picks the highest-Q one, scaling poorly with action dimension. All of these consult the critic either after a full action has been produced or via a separately trained auxiliary policy. Our method instead injects a noiseless-action Q-gradient into the Euler integrator at every denoising step, guiding the trajectory mid-integration without training an edit policy or modifying the base flow weights.
